text: Lesson 3 covered triage at the single-alert level: deciding fast whether one alert is a real threat or noise. That skill doesn't disappear once an alert is confirmed real - it's just the entry point. A real incident is almost never just that one alert. It's the alert that happened to fire first, sitting on top of a cluster of related activity.

Take an "impossible travel" alert - a sign-in from two distant locations minutes apart, confirmed real with no VPN or travel on record. Incident-scale triage asks what else is tied to that same account in the same window. Eleven minutes later, a new mailbox forwarding rule. Two minutes after that, an OAuth consent grant to an unfamiliar app. Twenty minutes later, a download from a shared finance folder. That's a confirmed account takeover with four related events, not one closed ticket.

Pulling every event tied to that one account into a single timeline turns an isolated alert into the real picture: one sign-in, one new mail rule, one app grant, one download, all inside 33 minutes. Each event on its own looks minor. Together, tied to the same entity, they describe exactly what an attacker did after getting in.

The practical move is grouping by entity instead of by alert ID. Confirm the first alert the same way Lesson 3 taught. Then pull every alert and raw event sharing that same account, host, or IP across every log source - identity, email, endpoint - into one working set, the same entity-based thinking behind Sentinel's investigation graph. Build that full picture before any containment decision gets made, because a decision made on an incomplete view is a decision made on bad information.

Closing one alert as confirmed-and-escalated without pulling its related mailbox-rule and OAuth-grant events is a common way real incidents get under-investigated. Next: timeline reconstruction, pulling events from firewall, endpoint, identity, and email logs into one chronological sequence to see the real attack progression.
